video_title: Bulkheads: Why Isolation Beats More Capacity
core_insight: Bulkheads isolate workloads with separate resource pools so one noisy or failing domain cannot starve others, trading utilization for containment.

scenes.voice: Why do we need bulkheads? Because a single shared pool means the loudest workload wins.
scenes.visual: Animated ship with one compartment flooding, then bulkhead walls containing water. Cut to server diagram with one shared thread pool being drained by a spiking service.

scenes.voice: In distributed systems, threads, connections, CPU are shared. A slow downstream API or traffic spike can block threads and starve unrelated services. That is cascading failure.
scenes.visual: Simple flow: Client → Load Balancer → Shared Thread Pool → Services. One service spikes, pool empties, other services stall. Red warning pulses.

scenes.voice: The obvious fix is add more capacity. More replicas help, but they don't stop sharing. A spike still consumes everything, just later.
scenes.visual: Pool grows larger but still single. Spike fills it again. Label: Scale out ≠ isolation.

scenes.voice: Bulkhead is intentional fragmentation. Separate pools per workload or dependency with hard limits and rejection at the boundary.
scenes.visual: Diagram splits into three isolated pools feeding same service. Show quotas.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR Client --> LB LB --> BulkheadA[Checkout Bulkhead
Pool: 50 threads] LB --> BulkheadB[Catalog Bulkhead
Pool: 200 threads] LB --> BulkheadC[Search Bulkhead
Pool: 100 threads] BulkheadA --> Service[Shared Service] BulkheadB --> Service BulkheadC --> Service

scenes.voice: Now a catalog spike fills its 200 threads, but checkout's 50 threads stay available. Saturation causes local rejection, not global collapse.
scenes.visual: Catalog pool fills red, Checkout pool stays green. Rejection icon at Catalog bulkhead boundary.

scenes.voice: Trade-off: you gain containment and SLO protection, you lose utilization. Idle capacity can exist in one bulkhead while another is overloaded. Sizing matters, and bulkheads don't fix a shared downstream bottleneck.
scenes.visual: Two pools: one empty, one full. Metrics show utilization vs isolation. Arrow to shared DB with warning.

scenes.voice: Use bulkheads when workloads share infrastructure but have different SLOs. Protect critical paths from non-critical ones. Isolation is a design choice, not an afterthought.
scenes.visual: E-commerce flash sale example: Checkout protected, Catalog and Recommendations isolated. Green check on Checkout SLO.

mental_model: Think of resources like ship compartments. Bulkheads are walls with quotas. When one compartment floods, the walls keep the rest afloat. Design for failure domains, not just total capacity.
final_takeaway: Bulkheads contain failure by isolating resources per workload. You trade utilization for safety.
